name: Omar Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at a big supermarket in the retail park, next to the furniture place and the gym. My main job is the fruit and veg section: rotating stock, checking dates, pulling out the soft tomatoes before anyone complains. When the queues build up they shout for me on the radio and I jump on a till. I've been there a year, and my manager says I'm good with customers but I still mess up the waste logs.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the early morning when the produce comes in and everything looks perfect for about an hour. What wears me out is the cold room and the chillers, my hands are always freezing. I live on my own in a rented flat, and I'm trying to save for a deposit, which at this rate takes about forever. On Thursdays I play five-a-side, and that keeps me sane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, the hype was overdone. At work I'd joke with the lads that we're safe for now, back to the tomatoes. Online, nothing, I mostly just watch football clips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't change my real problem, which is that rent eats nearly half my pay. I've got about three months saved, but the deposit for a flat is like two years of saving. If AI does nothing, I'm still renting at thirty-five unless I earn more somehow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job and ask about the supervisor training, because that's the only pay rise in sight. I'd keep saving about a hundred and fifty a month. And I've been reading about refrigeration engineers, the people who fix the chillers, so I might look into that course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, a bit flat. Not scared, just stuck in the same spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where did the fridge engineer idea come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our store has a fridge engineer, Kofi, who comes in every couple of weeks. He told me he earns about double what I do and he's always busy. I watched the fridge engineer fix a chiller in twenty minutes and thought, that's a real skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long would you stay on the produce section if nothing changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, maybe three. If I'm not a supervisor by then, I'd want to be doing a trade. I don't want to be the oldest guy pulling soft tomatoes off the shelf.

say: I'd say the **hype was overdone**, and joke that we're safe for now.
I'd keep quiet **online** and stick to football clips.
think: **Rent** eats nearly half my pay, whatever AI does.
A **flat deposit** is about two years of saving, so I'm stuck renting.
do: Ask about **supervisor training**, the only pay rise in sight.
feel: **Okay** but **flat**, stuck in the same spot.
S0.quote: I don't want to be the oldest guy pulling soft tomatoes off the shelf.
fieldNote: Omar's pressure is **rent and a deposit**, not technology.
A visiting **fridge engineer** gave him a concrete picture of a better job.
He sets himself a **two-to-three-year** deadline even in a quiet world.

steps.text: Ask the manager about supervisor training this year
Save about a hundred and fifty a month for a deposit
Find out about the refrigeration engineering course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening, so let's be practical about it. At work I'd say the people who learn the new systems will be fine. With friends I'd say it's not the end of the world, it's just change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the produce ordering is already half done by a computer, and in this picture it'd be fully done. The date checks and the price changes go to software. The computer would do the waste logs, which is the part I'm bad at anyway, but it also means fewer hours for people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the refrigeration course in the evenings within the next six months. I'd keep using the AI tools now and then, mainly to help me study, since my maths is rusty. I'd also stop going out on Saturdays and put that money toward course fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way that pushes me. Like a referee showing you a yellow card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would fewer hours look like for you exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new systems mean the store needs one person on produce at a time instead of two. Me and Callum share it now. One of us would go to the tills, and the tills are the part robots would take later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use the AI tools for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it like a tutor, ask it to explain how a compressor works, or test me before exams. I tried it once for a CV and it was good. I'm not going to trust it with everything, but for homework it's fine.

say: I'd say it's happening, so let's be **practical**.
I'd tell colleagues that people who **learn the new systems** will be fine.
think: Produce **ordering and waste logs** go fully to software.
Fewer tasks means **fewer hours**, and one of the two produce staff moves to tills.
do: Start the **refrigeration course** in the evenings within six months.
Use AI tools as a **study tutor** for my rusty maths.
Stop **Saturday nights out** to pay course fees.
feel: **Anxious**, but pushed forward like a **yellow card**.
S1.quote: The computer would do the waste logs, which is the part I'm bad at anyway, but it also means fewer hours for people like me.
fieldNote: Omar sees AI taking the **paperwork** side of his job first.
He's **steady**: uses AI as a tutor, not a crutch.
The real threat is the produce role shrinking to **one person**.

steps.text: Enrol in evening refrigeration engineering within six months
Use an AI tutor to revise maths for the course
Drop Saturday nights out to cover course fees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is serious, and the government and companies both need to do their part. No point blaming one side. At work I'd say get a trade, now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it's bad. In 2028 the thinking AI wipes out the office jobs, and loads of those people will want the same trade courses I want. Then around 2031 robots can do the shelves, the tills and the produce, and I'd be thirty with half a qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the refrigeration course immediately, full speed, even if I have to drop to part-time at the shop. I'd cut everything, maybe move back in with my mum to save the rent. I'd put the deposit dream on hold completely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. That's the word. Like the ground got pulled away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would moving back in with your mum feel like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd be humbling, honestly. My mum would be happy to have me back, but I left at twenty-one feeling like a grown-up. Saving six hundred a month in rent by moving back in with my mum is the difference between finishing the course and not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would fridge engineering be safe from robots in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit longer, because robots would also have to get into the back of a supermarket fridge, which is cramped and awkward. But someone would design a robot for that too. I'd have three or four years of real work, maybe.

say: I'd say the **government and companies** both need to act.
I'd tell colleagues to **get a trade**, now.
think: After **2028**, laid-off office workers chase the same trade courses.
Around **2031**, robots take shelves, tills and produce, while I'm half-qualified.
do: Start the **refrigeration course** at full speed, even dropping to part-time shifts.
Move back in with my **mum** to save the rent.
Put the **deposit** dream fully on hold.
S2.quote: Saving six hundred a month in rent by moving back in with my mum is the difference between finishing the course and not.
fieldNote: The **three-year gap** gives Omar time to train, but not much.
He'd give up **independence** and move home to fund the switch.
He guesses trades may last **a little longer**, but doesn't count on it.

steps.text: Start the refrigeration course full-time within months
Move out of the rented flat back to mum's
Shelve the plan to buy a flat
Ask mum for free rent while training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if you start now. At five-a-side I'd tell the lads to sort out a trade. I'd keep it practical, no doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is decent for me. Five years means I could be a qualified fridge engineer before the robots come for the supermarket shelves. Robots on the shop floor around 2034 means I'd be thirty-five, with a few years' experience as an engineer by then. It's still a race, but I'd be ahead of the office crowd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the refrigeration course over two years in the evenings, keep my shop job, and save about two hundred a month. I'd ask Kofi if I can shadow him on his rounds. And I'd keep using AI to help me study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but more in control. Like being two goals down at half-time, not five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Kofi actually let you shadow him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi would probably laugh, but he's said before that his firm is short of people. If I'm on the course, it shows I'm serious. That could turn into an apprenticeship with his firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound calmer. Is the worry still there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if I'm honest. It's still my job going, just later. And I don't know if fridges stay safe once the robots are good enough.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough if you start now.
I'd tell the **five-a-side** lads to sort out a trade.
think: Robots around **2034** means I could be a qualified **fridge engineer** first.
It's still a **race**, but I'd be ahead of office workers.
do: Do the **refrigeration course** over two years in the evenings.
Save about **£200 a month** while keeping the shop job.
Ask Kofi if I can **shadow him** on rounds.
feel: **Anxious** but **in control**, two goals down, not five.
S3.quote: Five years means I could be a qualified fridge engineer before the robots come for the supermarket shelves.
fieldNote: Five years gives Omar a **workable plan** with an apprenticeship route.
He admits the worry remains because his **shop job** still goes.
His **football metaphors** reflect a practical, centre-ground temperament.

steps.text: Complete a two-year evening refrigeration course
Save two hundred a month toward a cushion
Ask Kofi's firm about an apprenticeship
Use AI as a study tutor each week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a lot of time, and people should use it wisely. At work I'd say there's no rush, but don't sit still either. Pretty middle of the road, like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, for me this is fine. Robots on the shop floor around 2039, I'd be forty and a fridge engineer for years by then. The thinking AI in 2036 might change the paperwork side of engineering, but I'd have time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still take the refrigeration course, maybe starting next year instead of now. I'd keep saving for the deposit, because ten years is enough to buy a flat first. I'd keep the shop job for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I suppose. It's still coming. But it's like a storm on the forecast for next month, not this afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still go for the flat in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd still try. If I'm a fridge engineer by 2030, I'd earn enough for a mortgage. That's the plan, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly my mum and my sister. My sister is a receptionist at a dental clinic, and that's exactly the thinking work AI takes in 2036. I'd worry for her more than for me.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a lot, so use it wisely.
I'd tell colleagues there's **no rush**, but don't sit still.
think: Robots around **2039** means I'd be a fridge engineer for years by then.
Thinking AI in 2036 changes the **paperwork side** of engineering, with time to adjust.
do: Start the **refrigeration course** next year instead of now.
feel: **Uneasy**, like a storm forecast for **next month**.
S4.quote: My sister is a receptionist at a dental clinic, and that's exactly the thinking work AI takes in 2036.
fieldNote: With ten years, Omar puts the **flat** back in the plan.
His worry shifts to his sister's **receptionist job**, which is thinking work.
He calls himself **middle of the road**, matching his centre outlook.

steps.text: Start the refrigeration course next year
Keep saving each month for a flat deposit
Keep working produce and tills at the retail park

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd be competing with every office worker for the same trade courses, and I'd have about three years. What would help is free trade courses and a bit of money to live on while you do them, so people like me don't have to move back home.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people who stock shelves at night. They're the ones nobody sees, and they'd be the first ones replaced, I reckon. Somebody should talk to them.

headlineQuote: I watched the fridge engineer fix a chiller in twenty minutes and thought, that's a real skill.
portrait: Omar is **27**, a junior produce assistant who jumps on the **tills** at a retail park supermarket.
He rents alone, saves for a **flat deposit** and has about three months put by.
A visiting **fridge engineer** gave him a plan: refrigeration engineering.
He uses AI **now and then**, mainly as a study tutor.
His mood eases as the timeline lengthens; with two years he'd **move home** to fund training.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, competing with laid-off office workers for trade courses.
whatWouldHelp: **Free trade courses** with a little living money while studying.
